decks.title: Circles — Part 1: Tangents and the radius
goals: Tell a secant from a tangent and a line that misses the circle
State how many tangents pass through a point inside, on and outside a circle
Prove that the tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius
Use the right angle at the point of contact to find lengths and angles

slides.heading: Circles, Part 1: Tangents and the radius
slides.body_md: A line can miss a circle, cut it twice, or just **touch** it once.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and three horizontal lines: the top line misses the circle, the middle line touches it at exactly one point T, and the lower line cuts it at two points A and B.
visual.caption: Three positions of a line: no common point, one common point (tangent at $T$), two common points (secant through $A$ and $B$).

slides.narration: Welcome to Circles. Think of a cycle wheel resting on a road. The road touches the wheel at just one point. In this chapter that kind of line is called a tangent. We will see where tangents come from, prove the one fact that powers the whole chapter, and use it to find lengths and angles.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Name the three positions of a line and a circle
Count the tangents from a point **inside**, **on** and **outside** a circle
Prove: **tangent $\perp$ radius** at the point of contact
Find tangent lengths with Pythagoras
Find angles using the right angle at the point of contact
slides.narration: Here are your goals for part one. The chapter is short, but every question uses the same small set of facts. If you understand why the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, the rest follows naturally.

slides.heading: A line and a circle: three cases
slides.body_md: Let $d$ be the distance of the line from the centre $O$ and $r$ the radius.

visual.alt: Table: a line at a distance greater than the radius has no common point with the circle; at a distance equal to the radius it has one common point and is a tangent; at a distance less than the radius it has two and is a secant.
visual.caption: Compare the distance of the line from the centre with the radius.

slides.narration: Drop a perpendicular from the centre to the line, and call its length d. If d is more than the radius, the line misses the circle. If d is less, the line cuts the circle at two points and is called a secant. If d is exactly the radius, the line touches the circle at one point. That line is a tangent.

slides.heading: A tangent is the limit of secants
slides.body_md: Fix $P$ on the circle and let $Q$ slide along the circle towards $P$. The secant $PQ$ turns, and when $Q$ reaches $P$ it becomes the **tangent at $P$**. The common point is the **point of contact**.

visual.alt: A circle with a fixed point P at the bottom and three secants through P meeting the circle again at Q1, Q2 and Q3, each closer to P than the last; the horizontal tangent at P is the limiting position.
visual.caption: As $Q$ slides towards $P$, the secant $PQ$ turns into the tangent at $P$.

slides.narration: Here is another way to see a tangent. Fix a point P on the circle and draw a secant through P and a second point Q. Now slide Q towards P. The secant turns, and the two common points come closer. When they merge into one, the secant has become the tangent at P. There is exactly one tangent at each point.

slides.heading: Quick check: which kind of line?
slides.body_md: Compare the distance of the line from the centre with the radius.
slides.narration: Is the distance from the centre smaller than the radius, equal to it, or larger? That single comparison decides the answer.

slides.heading: How many tangents from a point?
slides.body_md: From a point **inside**: none. From a point **on** the circle: exactly one. From a point **outside**: exactly two.

visual.alt: Three equal circles. In the first, a point P lies inside and no tangent passes through it. In the second, a point Q lies on the circle with exactly one tangent. In the third, a point R lies outside with two tangents to the circle.
visual.caption: Number of tangents from a point: $0$ (inside), $1$ (on the circle), $2$ (outside).

slides.narration: Every line through an inside point cuts the circle twice, so no tangent passes through it. At a point on the circle there is exactly one tangent. From a point outside there are two, one touching each side of the circle. Remember the pattern: none, one, two.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: position of a line
slides.body_md: A circle has radius $5$ cm. Lines $l_1$, $l_2$, $l_3$ are $3$ cm, $5$ cm and $7$ cm from its centre. Describe each, and find the chord cut off by the secant.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $3 < 5$: $l_1$ is a **secant**.
**Step 2 —** $5 = 5$: $l_2$ is a **tangent**; $7 > 5$: $l_3$ misses the circle.
**Step 3 —** The perpendicular from $O$ bisects the chord: half-chord $= \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4$ cm.
**Answer —** The chord on $l_1$ is $8$ cm long.

visual.alt: Worked table: for a circle of radius 5 centimetres, a line 3 centimetres from the centre is a secant with a chord of 8 centimetres, a line 5 centimetres away is a tangent, and a line 7 centimetres away misses the circle.
visual.caption: Distance less than, equal to, or more than the radius.

slides.narration: Compare each distance with the radius: three is less than five, five equals five, and seven is more. So we have a secant, a tangent and a line that misses. For the chord, use the class nine fact that the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. Pythagoras gives half the chord as four, so the chord is eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Theorem: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius
slides.body_md: **Theorem.** The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

visual.alt: Circle with centre O and tangent XY at P. A point Q on the tangent is joined to O; the segment OQ crosses the circle at R, so OQ is longer than the radius OR, which equals OP. The radius OP is perpendicular to XY.
visual.caption: Theorem: the tangent at $P$ is perpendicular to the radius $OP$. $OQ > OR = OP$ for every other point $Q$ of the tangent.

slides.narration: Here is the key theorem of the chapter. The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. In the figure, the tangent X Y touches the circle at P, and the radius O P meets it at a right angle. Learn the statement exactly; it is examined as a proof.

slides.heading: Proof of the theorem
slides.body_md: **Given:** tangent $XY$ at $P$, centre $O$. **To prove:** $OP \perp XY$.
bullets: Take any point $Q$ on $XY$ other than $P$; join $OQ$
$Q$ lies **outside** the circle — otherwise $XY$ would cut the circle twice
So $OQ$ meets the circle at $R$, and $OQ > OR = OP$
$OP$ is the **shortest** segment from $O$ to $XY$
The shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular: $OP \perp XY$

nodes.label: Given: tangent $XY$ at $P$; to prove $OP \perp XY$
$Q$ is outside the circle (else $XY$ is a secant)
$OP$ is the shortest segment from $O$ to $XY$

visual.alt: Proof chain: take any other point Q on the tangent; it lies outside the circle, so O Q is longer than the radius; hence O P is the shortest segment from O to the tangent, and the shortest segment is the perpendicular.
visual.caption: The proof in five links.

slides.narration: Take any other point Q on the tangent. It cannot be inside the circle, or the line would be a secant. So Q is outside, and O Q is longer than the radius. That makes O P the shortest segment from O to the tangent. And the shortest segment from a point to a line is the perpendicular. That completes the proof.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a rope round a well
slides.body_md: A circular well in a Rajasthan village has radius $8$ m. A rope from a peg $Q$, $17$ m from the centre, is pulled taut so that it just touches the rim at $P$. How long is $QP$?
bullets: **Step 1 —** The rope touches the rim, so $QP$ is a tangent and $\angle OPQ = 90^\circ$.
**Step 2 —** In right $\triangle OPQ$ the hypotenuse is $OQ = 17$ m.

visual.alt: A circular well of radius 8 metres with centre O. A peg Q is 17 metres from O. A taut rope from Q touches the rim at P, making a right angle with the radius OP. The rope length PQ is unknown.
visual.caption: The rope $QP$ is a tangent, so $\angle OPQ = 90^\circ$.

slides.narration: The rope touches the rim, so it is a tangent, and the radius to the point of contact makes a right angle with it. Now it is just Pythagoras. Be careful: the hypotenuse is the line from the centre to the peg, seventeen metres, because it is opposite the right angle. So the rope is fifteen metres long.

slides.heading: Quick check: tangent length
slides.body_md: Find the right angle first, then decide which side is the hypotenuse.
slides.narration: Where is the right angle? The side opposite it is the hypotenuse. Then use Pythagoras.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: tangent and chord
slides.body_md: $ST$ is the tangent at $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, and $PQ$ is a chord with $\angle POQ = 110^\circ$. Find $\angle TPQ$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $OP = OQ$, so $\angle OPQ = \angle OQP = \dfrac{180^\circ - 110^\circ}{2} = 35^\circ$.
**Step 2 —** $\angle OPT = 90^\circ$ (tangent $\perp$ radius).
**Step 3 —** $\angle TPQ = 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$.
**Pattern —** The angle between the tangent and the chord is half the angle at the centre.

visual.alt: Circle with centre O; ST is the tangent at P. A chord PQ makes an angle with the tangent marked with a question mark, and the angle POQ at the centre is 110 degrees.
visual.caption: $\angle POQ = 110^\circ$ and $ST$ is the tangent at $P$. Find $\angle TPQ$.

slides.narration: Two facts do all the work. First, the triangle O P Q has two equal radii, so its base angles are equal, thirty five degrees each. Second, the tangent makes a right angle with the radius O P. Subtract to get fifty five degrees. Notice it is exactly half of one hundred and ten. That pattern always holds.

slides.heading: Two consequences of the theorem
slides.body_md: (1) The line perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact **passes through the centre**. (2) The tangents at the two ends of a diameter are **parallel**, $2r$ apart.

visual.alt: Circle with diameter AB. The tangent l at A and the tangent m at B are both perpendicular to AB, so they are parallel, and the distance between them is the diameter.
visual.caption: Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel; the distance between them is $2r$.

slides.narration: Two useful consequences. First, if you draw the perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact, it must pass through the centre, because the radius is already that perpendicular. Second, the tangents at the two ends of a diameter are both perpendicular to it, so they are parallel. The distance between them is the diameter.

slides.heading: Quick check: angle between tangent and chord
slides.body_md: Use the right angle and the isosceles triangle.
slides.narration: Start with the right angle between the tangent and the radius. Then use the two equal radii.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $d > r$: no common point; $d = r$: **tangent**; $d < r$: **secant**
Tangents from a point: none inside, one on, two outside
**Tangent $\perp$ radius** at the point of contact — prove it by "shortest distance"
Right triangle $OPQ$: hypotenuse is $OQ$, from the centre to the outside point
Tangent–chord angle $=$ half the angle at the centre

rows: Tangent $\perp$ radius at the point of contact
get a right angle, then Pythagoras or the angle sum
Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel
The perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through the centre
Tangents from a point: $0$ inside, $1$ on, $2$ outside

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel and 2 r apart, the perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through the centre, and the number of tangents from a point is 0, 1 or 2.
visual.caption: Every result in this chapter starts from the right angle at the point of contact.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Compare the distance of a line from the centre with the radius to name it. Count tangents from a point: none, one or two. Above all, the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. That right angle lets you use Pythagoras and angle sums in almost every question.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Theorem proof (3–5 marks):** given, to prove and figure 1 + point $Q$ outside 1 + $OQ > OP$ 1 + "shortest is perpendicular" 1
**Tangent length (2 marks):** right angle stated with reason 1 + Pythagoras and answer 1
**Mistake:** taking the tangent as the hypotenuse
**Mistake:** marking the right angle at the outside point instead of at the point of contact
**Mistake:** forgetting to write the reason "tangent $\perp$ radius"
slides.narration: In proofs, write given, to prove, and draw a neat figure; each earns credit. In numerical questions, always write the reason for the right angle: tangent perpendicular to radius. The most common slip is using the wrong hypotenuse. The hypotenuse always runs from the centre to the outside point.

decks.title: Circles — Part 2: Tangents from an external point
goals: Prove that the two tangents from an external point are equal
Use the angle facts: OP bisects the angles and the angle between the tangents is supplementary to the angle at the centre
Solve problems on quadrilaterals and triangles drawn round a circle
Combine both theorems in multi-step problems

slides.heading: Circles, Part 2: Tangents from an external point
slides.body_md: Two tangents, one point, and a surprising equality.

visual.alt: Circle with centre O and an external point P. Two tangents PA and PB touch the circle at A and B and are marked equal; the radii OA and OB meet them at right angles, and OP is joined.
visual.caption: Tangents from an external point are equal: $PA = PB$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. From a point outside a circle we can draw two tangents. Measure them and you will find they are always equal. In this part we prove that, and then use it to solve problems on triangles and quadrilaterals drawn around a circle, like a pond touching every wall of a park.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Prove: **tangents from an external point are equal**
Use: $OP$ bisects $\angle APB$; $\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180^\circ$
Prove and use $AB + CD = BC + DA$ for a quadrilateral round a circle
Find tangent lengths in a triangle round a circle
Show that a parallelogram round a circle is a rhombus
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. The second theorem is short to prove, and it unlocks a whole family of results. The board often asks for its proof, and then for a calculation that uses it.

slides.heading: Theorem: tangents from an external point are equal
slides.body_md: **Theorem.** The lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal: $PA = PB$.

visual.alt: Circle with centre O and an external point P. Two tangents PA and PB touch the circle at A and B and are marked equal; the radii OA and OB meet them at right angles, and OP is joined.
visual.caption: Tangents from an external point are equal: $PA = PB$.

slides.narration: Here is the theorem. The two tangents drawn from a point outside a circle have equal lengths. In the figure, P A equals P B. The radii O A and O B meet the tangents at right angles, because of the first theorem. That is the key to the proof.

slides.heading: Proof by RHS congruence
slides.body_md: **Given:** $PA$, $PB$ tangents from $P$; centre $O$. **To prove:** $PA = PB$. **Join** $OA$, $OB$, $OP$.
bullets: $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$ (tangent $\perp$ radius)
$OA = OB$ (radii)
$OP = OP$ (common hypotenuse)
$\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$ (RHS), so $PA = PB$ (CPCT)

visual.alt: Circle with centre O and an external point P. Two tangents PA and PB touch the circle at A and B and are marked equal; the radii OA and OB meet them at right angles, and OP is joined.
visual.caption: Tangents from an external point are equal: $PA = PB$.

slides.narration: Join O to A, B and P. The angles at A and B are right angles by the first theorem. The radii O A and O B are equal, and the hypotenuse O P is shared. So the two right triangles are congruent by R H S, and the corresponding sides P A and P B are equal. Four lines, four marks.

slides.heading: What else the congruence gives
slides.body_md: From $\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$: $OP$ **bisects** $\angle APB$ and $\angle AOB$. In $OAPB$ two angles are $90^\circ$, so $\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180^\circ$. Also $AB \perp OP$.

visual.alt: Two tangents from P make an angle of 60 degrees; the angle AOB at the centre is 120 degrees. OP bisects both angles and the chord AB is perpendicular to OP.
visual.caption: $\angle APB + \angle AOB = 60^\circ + 120^\circ = 180^\circ$, and $OP$ bisects both angles.

slides.narration: The same congruence gives more. The angles at P are equal, so O P bisects the angle between the tangents, and it also bisects the angle at the centre. The quadrilateral O A P B has two right angles, so the other two angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees. Here, sixty and one hundred and twenty.

slides.heading: Quick check: angle at the centre
slides.body_md: Use the angle sum of the quadrilateral $OAPB$.
slides.narration: Two angles of the quadrilateral are right angles. What must the other two add up to?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: lengths
slides.body_md: From $P$, $10$ cm from the centre of a circle of radius $6$ cm, tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn. Find $PA$ and the length of the chord $AB$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$: $PA = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8$ cm, and $PB = PA = 8$ cm.
**Step 2 —** $AB \perp OP$ at $M$. Area of $\triangle OAP$: $\dfrac12 \times 6 \times 8 = \dfrac12 \times 10 \times AM$.

visual.alt: Circle of radius 6 centimetres with centre O; P is 10 centimetres from O. Tangents PA and PB are drawn; the length PA is unknown.
visual.caption: Radius $6$ cm, $OP = 10$ cm. Find $PA$.

slides.narration: Start with the right angle at A and Pythagoras: P A is eight centimetres, and P B is the same. For the chord, remember that A B is perpendicular to O P. Write the area of triangle O A P in two ways, once with base O A and once with base O P. That gives half the chord, four point eight, so the chord is nine point six.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: angles
slides.body_md: Tangents $PA$ and $PB$ meet at $P$ with $\angle APB = 50^\circ$. Find $\angle PAB$ and $\angle OAB$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $PA = PB$, so $\angle PAB = \angle PBA = \dfrac{180^\circ - 50^\circ}{2} = 65^\circ$.
**Step 2 —** $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, so $\angle OAB = 90^\circ - 65^\circ = 25^\circ$.
**Pattern —** $\angle OAB = \dfrac12 \angle APB$ always.
**Check —** $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - 50^\circ = 130^\circ$, and in isosceles $\triangle OAB$: $\dfrac{180^\circ - 130^\circ}{2} = 25^\circ$ ✓.

visual.alt: Two tangents from P to a circle with centre O meet at an angle of 50 degrees. The chord AB is drawn and the angle OAB is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: Tangents $PA$, $PB$ with $\angle APB = 50^\circ$. Find $\angle OAB$.

slides.narration: Because the tangents are equal, triangle P A B is isosceles, so each base angle is sixty five degrees. The radius makes a right angle with the tangent at A, so the angle O A B is ninety minus sixty five, twenty five degrees. Check it another way, through the angle at the centre. Both routes agree.

slides.heading: A quadrilateral round a circle
slides.body_md: If a circle touches all four sides of $ABCD$ at $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, then $AB + CD = BC + DA$.
bullets: Equal tangents: $AP = AS$, $BP = BQ$, $CR = CQ$, $DR = DS$
Add: $(AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)$
So $AB + CD = AD + BC$

visual.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD drawn around a circle that touches its sides at P, Q, R and S. AB is 7 centimetres, BC is 9 centimetres, CD is 8 centimetres and DA is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: $ABCD$ circumscribes the circle: $AB + CD = BC + DA$.

slides.narration: Now draw a quadrilateral around a circle. Each vertex sends out two equal tangents. Add the four pieces that make up A B and C D, then regroup them into A D and B C. The sums of opposite sides come out equal. This proof is short and is a favourite in board papers.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the missing side
slides.body_md: In the figure, $AB = 7$ cm, $BC = 9$ cm, $CD = 8$ cm. Find $DA$. If $AP = 3$ cm, find the tangent lengths from $B$, $C$ and $D$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $AB + CD = BC + DA$: $7 + 8 = 9 + DA$, so $DA = 6$ cm.
**Check —** $AS = DA - DS = 6 - 3 = 3 = AP$ ✓.

visual.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD drawn around a circle that touches its sides at P, Q, R and S. AB is 7 centimetres, BC is 9 centimetres, CD is 8 centimetres and DA is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: $ABCD$ circumscribes the circle: $AB + CD = BC + DA$.

slides.narration: The opposite-sides rule gives the missing side at once: six centimetres. If one tangent length is known, walk around the quadrilateral. Each side minus the tangent already known gives the next tangent. When you come back to A, you should get the length you started with. That final check catches arithmetic slips.

slides.heading: Quick check: circumscribed quadrilateral
slides.body_md: Pair the opposite sides correctly.
slides.narration: Which sides are opposite? Their sums must be equal.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a triangle round a circle
slides.body_md: The incircle of $\triangle ABC$ touches $BC$ at $D$, $CA$ at $E$, $AB$ at $F$, with $BD = 6$ cm, $DC = 8$ cm and $AB = 10$ cm. Find $AC$ and the perimeter.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $BF = BD = 6$ cm, so $AF = 10 - 6 = 4$ cm.
**Step 2 —** $AE = AF = 4$ cm and $CE = CD = 8$ cm.
**Shortcut —** tangent from a vertex $=$ semi-perimeter $-$ opposite side: $AF = 18 - 14 = 4$ ✓.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with a circle inside touching BC at D, CA at E and AB at F. AB is 10 centimetres, BD is 6 centimetres, DC is 8 centimetres, and AC is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: The incircle touches $BC$ at $D$: $BD = 6$ cm, $DC = 8$ cm, $AB = 10$ cm.

slides.narration: Each vertex sends out two equal tangents. From B, both are six. So A F is four, and A E is also four. From C, both tangents are eight. Add them to get A C, twelve centimetres. A neat shortcut: the tangent from any vertex equals the semi-perimeter minus the side opposite that vertex.

slides.heading: Quick check: perimeter from tangent lengths
slides.body_md: Each tangent length appears twice in the perimeter.
slides.narration: Write each side as the sum of two tangent lengths. How many times does each tangent length appear?

slides.heading: A parallelogram round a circle is a rhombus
slides.body_md: If parallelogram $ABCD$ circumscribes a circle: $AB + CD = BC + DA$ with $AB = CD$, $BC = DA$, so $2AB = 2BC$ and **all four sides are equal**.

visual.alt: A parallelogram ABCD drawn around a circle. All four sides are marked equal, showing that it must be a rhombus.
visual.caption: A parallelogram that circumscribes a circle has $AB + CD = BC + DA$, so all its sides are equal: a rhombus.

slides.narration: Combine the opposite-sides rule with what you know about parallelograms. Opposite sides are equal, so the rule becomes two A B equals two B C. All four sides are equal, so the parallelogram must be a rhombus. A rectangle that is not a square can never be drawn around a circle.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a path past a pool
slides.body_md: A circular park in Pune has radius $25$ m, and a circular pool with the same centre has radius $7$ m. A straight path $AB$ crosses the park and just touches the pool at $M$. Find the length of the path.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $OM \perp AB$ (radius $\perp$ tangent).
**Step 2 —** $\triangle OMA \cong \triangle OMB$ (RHS), so $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$.
**Answer —** $AB = 48$ m.

visual.alt: Two circles with the same centre O: a park of radius 25 metres and a pool of radius 7 metres. A straight path AB across the park touches the pool at M; OM is perpendicular to AB.
visual.caption: The path $AB$ touches the pool at $M$, so $OM \perp AB$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$.

slides.narration: The path touches the pool, so it is a tangent to the small circle, and O M is perpendicular to it. For the big circle, the same path is a chord, and the perpendicular from the centre bisects it. Pythagoras in triangle O M A gives twenty four metres, so the whole path is forty eight metres.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: **Tangents from an external point are equal** — proof by RHS
$OP$ bisects $\angle APB$ and $\angle AOB$; $\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180^\circ$
Quadrilateral round a circle: $AB + CD = BC + DA$
Triangle round a circle: tangent from a vertex $= s -$ opposite side
Parallelogram round a circle is a rhombus

rows: tangent from a vertex $=$ semi-perimeter $-$ opposite side

visual.alt: Summary table of part two: tangents from a point are equal and O P bisects the angles; the angle between the tangents and the angle at the centre add to 180 degrees; a circumscribed quadrilateral has equal sums of opposite sides; in a circumscribed triangle the tangent from a vertex is the semi-perimeter minus the opposite side; a circumscribed parallelogram is a rhombus.
visual.caption: One theorem, many consequences.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Tangents from an outside point are equal, proved by R H S. The line to the centre bisects the angles, and the angle between the tangents is supplementary to the angle at the centre. For figures drawn around a circle, mark the equal tangents from every vertex and the rest is addition.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Equal tangents proof (3 marks):** figure with radii joined 1 + right angles and RHS 1 + conclusion 1
**Quadrilateral proof (3 marks):** four pairs of equal tangents 1 + adding and regrouping 1 + conclusion 1
**Mistake:** writing $\angle APB = \angle AOB$ instead of supplementary
**Mistake:** pairing adjacent sides in $AB + CD = BC + DA$
**Mistake:** in a triangle, subtracting the wrong side from the semi-perimeter
slides.narration: In proofs, join the radii in your figure and state the right angles with the reason. Name the congruence rule, R H S. In quadrilateral problems, write the four pairs of equal tangents before adding. Watch the classic slips: the angles at P and O are supplementary, not equal, and opposite sides, not adjacent sides, have equal sums.

notes.title: Circles — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Lines and circles
sections.body_md:
Let $d$ be the distance of a line from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $r$.

- $d > r$: the line has **no common point** with the circle.
- $d = r$: exactly **one** common point — the line is a **tangent**, and the common point is the **point of contact**.
- $d < r$: **two** common points — the line is a **secant**.

A tangent is the limiting position of a secant $PQ$ as $Q$ moves along the circle to $P$. At each point of a circle there is exactly one tangent.

**Number of tangents from a point:** none from a point inside, exactly one from a point on the circle, exactly two from a point outside.

key_terms.definition_md: A line that meets a circle at exactly one point.
A line that meets a circle at two distinct points.
The common point of a tangent and the circle.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and three horizontal lines: the top line misses the circle, the middle line touches it at exactly one point T, and the lower line cuts it at two points A and B.
visual.caption: Three positions of a line: no common point, one common point (tangent at $T$), two common points (secant through $A$ and $B$).

visuals.alt: Three equal circles. In the first, a point P lies inside and no tangent passes through it. In the second, a point Q lies on the circle with exactly one tangent. In the third, a point R lies outside with two tangents to the circle.

sections.heading: 2. Theorem: tangent ⟂ radius
sections.body_md:
**Theorem 1.** The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

**Proof.** Let $XY$ be the tangent at $P$. Take any point $Q \ne P$ on $XY$. $Q$ lies outside the circle (otherwise $XY$ would be a secant), so $OQ$ meets the circle at $R$ with $OQ > OR = OP$. Hence $OP$ is the shortest segment from $O$ to $XY$, and the shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular to it: $OP \perp XY$.

**Consequences.**
- The perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through the centre.
- The tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel; the distance between two parallel tangents is the diameter.

sections.heading: 3. Using the right angle
sections.body_md:
At the point of contact $P$ of a tangent from an outside point $Q$, $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$, with **hypotenuse $OQ$**:

$$OQ^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2.$$

*Example:* radius $8$ m, $OQ = 17$ m gives the tangent $\sqrt{289 - 64} = 15$ m.

**Angles.** If $PQ$ is a chord and $PT$ the tangent at $P$, then $\angle OPQ = 90^\circ - \angle TPQ$, and the isosceles triangle $OPQ$ gives $\angle POQ = 2\angle TPQ$.

*Example:* $\angle POQ = 110^\circ$ gives $\angle TPQ = 55^\circ$.

**Concentric circles.** A chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller one is bisected at the point of contact: half-chord $= \sqrt{R^2 - r^2}$.

sections.heading: 5. Polygons drawn round a circle
sections.body_md:
Mark the two equal tangents from every vertex, then add.

**Quadrilateral** $ABCD$ touching the circle at $P, Q, R, S$: $AB + CD = BC + DA$, and the perimeter is $2(AB + CD)$.

**Triangle** $ABC$ with incircle touching $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$: if the tangent lengths are $x$ (from $A$), $y$ (from $B$), $z$ (from $C$), then $x + y = AB$, $y + z = BC$, $z + x = CA$, and $x + y + z = s$ (the semi-perimeter). So

$$x = s - BC, \quad y = s - CA, \quad z = s - AB.$$

*Example:* $AB = 10$, $BD = 6$, $DC = 8$ gives $AF = 4$ and $AC = 12$.

**Area and inradius:** joining the centre to the vertices splits the triangle into three triangles of height $r$, so area $= r \times s$.

sections.heading: 6. Special results worth remembering
sections.body_md:
- A **parallelogram** that circumscribes a circle is a **rhombus** ($2AB = 2BC$). So a rectangle round a circle must be a square.
- In a triangle **right-angled at $C$** with legs $a$, $b$ and hypotenuse $c$, the inradius is $r = \dfrac{a + b - c}{2}$ (the corner at $C$ forms a square of side $r$). *Example:* $8$, $15$, $17$ gives $r = 3$.
- In an **isosceles** triangle round a circle, the circle touches the base at its midpoint, and the vertex, the centre and that midpoint are collinear.
- The two tangents at the ends of a chord $PQ$ meet on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$, which passes through the centre.

visual.caption: A parallelogram that circumscribes a circle has $AB + CD = BC + DA$, so all its sides are equal: a rhombus.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Theorem proofs (3–5 marks):* given, to prove and a labelled figure 1; each justified step 1; conclusion 1. Name the reasons: "tangent $\perp$ radius", "RHS", "CPCT".
- *Lengths (2–3 marks):* right angle with reason 1; Pythagoras with the correct hypotenuse 1; answer with unit 1.
- *Angles (1–3 marks):* right angle at the point of contact, isosceles triangles from equal radii or equal tangents, angle sums.
- *Circumscribed figures (2–3 marks):* list the equal tangents, then add.

**Common mistakes**
1. Taking the tangent as the hypotenuse (it is always $OQ$, from the centre to the outside point).
2. Writing $\angle APB = \angle AOB$: they are supplementary.
3. Pairing adjacent sides in $AB + CD = BC + DA$.
4. Forgetting that a point inside the circle has no tangent.
5. Skipping the reason for a right angle in a proof.

cards.front_md: What is a **tangent** to a circle?
cards.back_md: A line that meets the circle at exactly one point.

cards.front_md: What is a **secant**?
cards.back_md: A line that meets the circle at two distinct points.

cards.front_md: The common point of a tangent and a circle is called…
cards.back_md: The point of contact.

cards.front_md: A line is at distance $d$ from the centre of a circle of radius $r$. When is it a tangent?
cards.back_md: When $d = r$ ($d < r$: secant; $d > r$: no common point).

cards.front_md: Number of tangents from a point inside / on / outside a circle?
How many tangents does a circle have at one point on it?
cards.back_md: Exactly one.

cards.front_md: A tangent as a limit of secants?
cards.back_md: As $Q \to P$ along the circle, the secant $PQ$ turns into the tangent at $P$.

cards.front_md: Theorem 1 (statement)?
cards.back_md: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

cards.front_md: Key idea of the proof of Theorem 1?
cards.back_md: Every other point of the tangent is outside, so $OP$ is the shortest segment from $O$ to the line, hence perpendicular.

cards.front_md: In right $\triangle OPQ$ ($PQ$ tangent at $P$), which side is the hypotenuse?
cards.back_md: $OQ$ — from the centre to the outside point.

cards.front_md: Radius $8$ m, $OQ = 17$ m. Tangent length?
Tangents at the ends of a diameter are…
cards.back_md: Parallel; the distance between them is the diameter.

cards.front_md: The perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through…
cards.back_md: The centre of the circle.

cards.front_md: Tangent $PT$ and chord $PQ$: relation between $\angle TPQ$ and $\angle POQ$?
cards.back_md: $\angle POQ = 2\angle TPQ$

cards.front_md: Chord of the larger of two concentric circles (radii $R > r$) touching the smaller?
cards.back_md: $2\sqrt{R^2 - r^2}$, bisected at the point of contact.

cards.front_md: Theorem 2 (statement)?
cards.back_md: The tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length.

cards.front_md: Proof of Theorem 2 in one line?
cards.back_md: $\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$ by RHS (right angles at $A$, $B$; $OA = OB$; $OP$ common).

cards.front_md: Tangents $PA$, $PB$: relation between $\angle APB$ and $\angle AOB$?
cards.back_md: They add up to $180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Tangents $PA$, $PB$: what does $OP$ bisect?
cards.back_md: Both $\angle APB$ and $\angle AOB$; also $AB \perp OP$.

cards.front_md: $\angle APB = 50^\circ$. Find $\angle OAB$.
cards.back_md: $25^\circ$ (half of $\angle APB$).

cards.front_md: $\angle APB = 90^\circ$, radius $r$. Shape of $OAPB$ and $OP$?
cards.back_md: A square; $OP = r\sqrt2$.

cards.front_md: $\angle APB = 60^\circ$, radius $r$. Find $OP$.
cards.back_md: $OP = 2r$ (since $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac12$).

cards.front_md: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ circumscribes a circle. Relation between sides?
cards.back_md: $AB + CD = BC + DA$

cards.front_md: Triangle round a circle: tangent from vertex $A$?
cards.back_md: $s - BC$, where $s$ is the semi-perimeter.

cards.front_md: A parallelogram circumscribes a circle. What kind of parallelogram is it?
cards.back_md: A rhombus.

cards.front_md: Can a non-square rectangle circumscribe a circle?
cards.back_md: No — a circumscribed parallelogram must have all sides equal.

cards.front_md: Inradius of a right triangle with legs $a$, $b$, hypotenuse $c$?
cards.back_md: $r = \dfrac{a + b - c}{2}$

cards.front_md: Area of a triangle in terms of its inradius $r$?
cards.back_md: Area $= r \times s$ ($s$ = semi-perimeter).

cards.front_md: Common slip with $\angle APB$ and $\angle AOB$?
cards.back_md: Writing them equal — they are supplementary.

questions.stem_md: A tangent to a circle meets the circle at
questions.solution_md: By definition a tangent **touches** the circle: it has exactly one point in common with it, the point of contact. A line meeting the circle at two points is a secant (b); a line with no common point (c) does not meet the circle at all.

questions.stem_md: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point that lies inside the circle?
questions.solution_md: Every line through an interior point cuts the circle at two points, so every such line is a secant. No tangent passes through a point inside the circle. (From a point **on** the circle there is exactly one tangent; from a point outside, exactly two.)

questions.stem_md: A line that meets a circle at two distinct points is called
questions.solution_md: A line with two common points with the circle is a **secant**. A tangent has one common point; a radius and a diameter are segments through the centre, not lines that just "meet" the circle.

questions.stem_md: The centre of a circle of radius $5$ cm is at a distance of $5$ cm from a line $l$. Then $l$ is

options.text_md: a line that does not meet the circle

questions.solution_md: Compare the distance $d$ of the line from the centre with the radius $r$: $d < r$ secant, $d = r$ tangent, $d > r$ no common point. Here $d = r = 5$ cm, so $l$ touches the circle at the foot of the perpendicular from the centre: a **tangent**.

questions.stem_md: $PQ$ is a tangent at $P$ to a circle with centre $O$ and radius $10$ cm. If $OQ = 26$ cm, then $PQ$ is
questions.solution_md: $OP \perp PQ$, so $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$ with hypotenuse $OQ$: $PQ = \sqrt{26^2 - 10^2} = \sqrt{676 - 100} = \sqrt{576} = 24$ cm. Option (d) adds the squares, treating $PQ$ as the hypotenuse; (b) and (c) subtract or add the lengths.

questions.stem_md: $PT$ is a tangent at $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, and $T$ is a point on the tangent with $\angle OTP = 35^\circ$. Then $\angle POT$ is
questions.solution_md: The radius $OP$ is perpendicular to the tangent, so $\angle OPT = 90^\circ$. In $\triangle OPT$: $\angle POT = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$. Option (d) forgets the right angle.

questions.stem_md: The tangents drawn at the two ends of a diameter of a circle are
questions.solution_md: Each tangent is perpendicular to the diameter $AB$ (radius $\perp$ tangent at the point of contact). Two lines perpendicular to the same line make equal alternate angles ($90^\circ$ each) with it, so they are **parallel**. They never meet, so (d), (a) and (b) are impossible.

questions.stem_md: $PT$ is the tangent at $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, and $PR$ is a chord with $\angle TPR = 50^\circ$. Then $\angle POR$ is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $\angle OPT = 90^\circ$, so $\angle OPR = 90^\circ - 50^\circ = 40^\circ$.

**Step 2.** $OP = OR$ (radii), so $\angle ORP = 40^\circ$.

**Step 3.** $\angle POR = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 40^\circ = 100^\circ$, twice the angle between the tangent and the chord. Option (b) stops at $\angle OPR + \angle ORP$.

questions.stem_md: From a point $P$, two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to a circle. If $PA = 7$ cm and $\angle APB = 60^\circ$, then the chord $AB$ is
questions.solution_md: $PA = PB$ (tangents from an external point), so $\triangle PAB$ is isosceles and $\angle PAB = \angle PBA = \dfrac{180^\circ - 60^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ$. All angles are $60^\circ$: the triangle is equilateral and $AB = PA = 7$ cm.

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. If $\angle APB = 70^\circ$, then $\angle AOB$ is
questions.solution_md: In quadrilateral $OAPB$, $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$. The angle sum is $360^\circ$, so $\angle AOB = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 70^\circ = 110^\circ$: the two angles are **supplementary**.

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, and $\angle AOB = 130^\circ$. Then $\angle PAB$ is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $\angle APB = 180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ$.

**Step 2.** $PA = PB$, so $\angle PAB = \angle PBA = \dfrac{180^\circ - 50^\circ}{2} = 65^\circ$.

Option (d) is $\angle APB$; option (a) is $\angle OAB$.

questions.stem_md: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is drawn to circumscribe a circle. If $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = 7$ cm and $CD = 5$ cm, then $AD$ is
questions.solution_md: For a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle, $AB + CD = BC + AD$. So $6 + 5 = 7 + AD$ and $AD = 4$ cm. Option (a) pairs the sides wrongly ($AB + BC - CD$).

questions.stem_md: A circle is inscribed in $\triangle ABC$, touching $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at $D$, $E$ and $F$. If $AF = 4$ cm, $BD = 5$ cm and $CE = 6$ cm, the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ is
questions.solution_md: Tangents from a vertex are equal: $AE = AF = 4$, $BF = BD = 5$, $CD = CE = 6$. Each tangent length is used twice, so the perimeter is $2(4 + 5 + 6) = 30$ cm. Option (b) counts each length once.

questions.stem_md: A circle is inscribed in a parallelogram $ABCD$ (it touches all four sides). If $AB = 8$ cm, then $BC$ is

options.text_md: impossible to find from the data

questions.solution_md: Since the parallelogram circumscribes a circle, $AB + CD = BC + DA$. In a parallelogram $AB = CD$ and $BC = DA$, so $2AB = 2BC$ and $BC = AB = 8$ cm: the parallelogram is a **rhombus**. Option (a) misses this hidden condition.

questions.stem_md: The distance between two parallel tangents of a circle is $18$ cm. The radius of the circle is
questions.solution_md: Two parallel tangents touch the circle at the ends of a diameter (the radii to the points of contact are both perpendicular to the same direction). So the distance between them is the diameter: $2r = 18$ and $r = 9$ cm.

questions.stem_md: From a point $Q$ at a distance of $29$ cm from the centre of a circle, the length of the tangent is $21$ cm. The **diameter** of the circle is
questions.solution_md: Radius $= \sqrt{29^2 - 21^2} = \sqrt{841 - 441} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ cm, so the diameter is $40$ cm. Option (a) stops at the radius; (b) and (c) subtract or add the lengths.

questions.stem_md: Two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$ such that $\angle APB = 90^\circ$. If $OA = 5$ cm, then $OP$ is
questions.solution_md: In $OAPB$, $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = \angle APB = 90^\circ$, so the fourth angle $\angle AOB$ is also $90^\circ$. With $OA = OB$, the rectangle $OAPB$ has equal adjacent sides: it is a square of side $5$ cm, and $OP$ is its diagonal: $OP = \sqrt{25 + 25} = 5\sqrt2$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A line touches a circle with centre $O$ and radius $9$ cm at $P$. $Q$ is a point on the line with $PQ = 12$ cm. Then $OQ$ is
questions.solution_md: $\angle OPQ = 90^\circ$, so $OQ$ is the hypotenuse: $OQ = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm. Option (d) subtracts the squares.

**Reason (R):** A line is a tangent to a circle when its distance from the centre equals the radius.

questions.stem_md: Exactly one tangent can be drawn to a circle at a point that lies on the circle.
questions.solution_md: The tangent at $P$ must be perpendicular to the radius $OP$, and through $P$ there is exactly one line perpendicular to $OP$. So the tangent at a point of the circle is unique.

questions.stem_md: If the radius of a circle is $5$ cm and the length of the tangent from a point $P$ is $12$ cm, then $P$ is $17$ cm from the centre.
questions.solution_md: The radius and the tangent are perpendicular, so the distance is the hypotenuse: $\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm, not $17$ cm. Adding the two lengths is the mistake.

questions.stem_md: If $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, then $\angle AOP = \angle BOP$.
questions.solution_md: $\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$ by RHS ($\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$, hypotenuse $OP$ common, $OA = OB$). So $\angle AOP = \angle BOP$: $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB$ (and $\angle APB$).

questions.stem_md: A secant can meet a circle at three points.
questions.solution_md: A line meets a circle at **at most two** points. A secant meets it at exactly two points.

questions.stem_md: If a circle inscribed in $\triangle ABC$ touches $AB$ at $F$, then $AF = BF$ for every triangle.
questions.solution_md: $AF$ equals the tangent from $A$ and $BF$ the tangent from $B$; these are equal only when $CA = CB$. Counter-example: $AB = 13$, $BC = 14$, $CA = 15$ cm gives $AF = 7$ cm and $BF = 6$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A line that touches a circle at exactly one point is called a ___ to the circle.
questions.solution_md: Such a line is a **tangent**; the common point is the point of contact.

questions.stem_md: The common point of a tangent and a circle is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the **point of contact** (also called the point of tangency).

questions.stem_md: The angle between a tangent to a circle and the radius through the point of contact is ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: The tangent at any point is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact: the angle is $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Two radii of a circle make an angle of $124^\circ$ with each other. The tangents drawn at their outer ends meet at a point outside the circle, where they make an angle of ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: Each tangent is perpendicular to its radius, so the quadrilateral formed by the two radii and the two tangents has two right angles. Its angles add up to $360^\circ$: the angle between the tangents $= 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 124^\circ = 56^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A circle inscribed in $\triangle ABC$ touches $BC$ at $D$, $CA$ at $E$ and $AB$ at $F$. If $BF = 4$ cm and $CE = 5$ cm, then $BC =$ ___ cm.
questions.solution_md: $BD = BF = 4$ cm and $CD = CE = 5$ cm (tangents from a point are equal), so $BC = BD + DC = 9$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The radius of a circle is $12$ cm and a point $Q$ is $37$ cm from its centre. Find the length (in cm) of the tangent drawn from $Q$ to the circle.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** The tangent $QP$ is perpendicular to the radius $OP$, so $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$ with hypotenuse $OQ = 37$ cm.

**Step 2.** $QP = \sqrt{37^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{1369 - 144} = \sqrt{1225} = 35$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: Right angle at the point of contact, Pythagoras set up

questions.stem_md: The length of the tangent from a point $P$ to a circle is $30$ cm, and $P$ is $34$ cm from the centre. Find the radius of the circle in cm.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Radius $\perp$ tangent, and $OP = 34$ cm is the hypotenuse.

**Step 2.** $r = \sqrt{34^2 - 30^2} = \sqrt{1156 - 900} = \sqrt{256} = 16$ cm.

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, and $\angle APB = 72^\circ$. Find $\angle OAB$ in degrees.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $PA = PB$, so $\angle PAB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 72^\circ}{2} = 54^\circ$.

**Step 2.** $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, so $\angle OAB = 90^\circ - 54^\circ = 36^\circ$ (half of $\angle APB$).

questions.stem_md: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ circumscribes a circle, with $AB = 9.5$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm and $CD = 7.5$ cm. Find $AD$ in cm.
A circle is inscribed in $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = 12$ cm, $BC = 15$ cm and $CA = 11$ cm. It touches $BC$ at $D$. Find $BD$ in cm.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Let the tangent lengths from $A$, $B$, $C$ be $x$, $y$, $z$. Then $x + y = 12$, $y + z = 15$, $z + x = 11$.

**Step 2.** Adding, $2(x + y + z) = 38$, so $x + y + z = 19$. Then $y = 19 - 11 = 8$. Hence $BD = 8$ cm (and $CD = 7$ cm, $AF = 4$ cm).

questions.stem_md: Two concentric circles have radii $17$ cm and $8$ cm. Find the length (in cm) of the chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Let the chord $AB$ touch the small circle at $M$. Then $OM \perp AB$ (radius $\perp$ tangent), and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.

**Step 2.** $AM = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{289 - 64} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm, so $AB = 2 \times 15 = 30$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: OM ⟂ AB and AM by Pythagoras

questions.stem_md: The tangent $PT$ from a point $P$ to a circle is $9$ cm long. The line from $P$ to the centre $O$ meets the circle first at $Q$, with $PQ = 3$ cm. Find the radius of the circle in cm.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $OP = r + 3$ and $\angle OTP = 90^\circ$, so $(r + 3)^2 = r^2 + 9^2$.

**Step 2.** $r^2 + 6r + 9 = r^2 + 81 \Rightarrow 6r = 72 \Rightarrow r = 12$ cm. **Check:** $15^2 = 225 = 144 + 81$ ✓.

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$ and radius $9$ cm. If $OP = 15$ cm, find the area of the quadrilateral $OAPB$ in cm².
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $PA = \sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm.

**Step 2.** $OP$ splits $OAPB$ into two congruent right triangles, each of area $\dfrac12 \times 9 \times 12 = 54$ cm². Area $= 2 \times 54 = 108$ cm².

questions.stem_md: Two tangents drawn from a point $P$ to a circle of radius $8$ cm are inclined to each other at $60^\circ$. Find the distance of $P$ from the centre, in cm.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $OP$ bisects the angle between the tangents, so $\angle OPA = 30^\circ$, and $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$.

**Step 2.** $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{OA}{OP}$, so $OP = \dfrac{8}{1/2} = 16$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle with centre $O$, and let $l$ and $m$ be the tangents at $A$ and $B$.

The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through it, so $OA \perp l$ and $OB \perp m$. Hence $l$ and $m$ make angles of $90^\circ$ with the line $AB$ on opposite sides, i.e. a pair of equal alternate angles with the transversal $AB$.

So $l \parallel m$.

questions.solution_md: Use the tangent–radius theorem twice, then the alternate-angles test for parallel lines.

marking_scheme.step: OA ⟂ l and OB ⟂ m (tangent ⟂ radius)
Equal alternate angles, hence l ∥ m

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from an external point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. If $\angle PAB = 62^\circ$, find $\angle APB$ and $\angle AOB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$PA = PB$ (tangents from an external point), so $\angle PBA = \angle PAB = 62^\circ$ and $\angle APB = 180^\circ - 124^\circ = 56^\circ$.

In $OAPB$, $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$, so $\angle AOB = 360^\circ - 180^\circ - 56^\circ = 124^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: The angle between the tangents and the angle at the centre are supplementary: $56^\circ + 124^\circ = 180^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A circle touches all four sides of a quadrilateral $ABCD$, with $AB = 11$ cm, $BC = 9$ cm and $CD = 7$ cm. Find $AD$ and the perimeter of $ABCD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
For a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle, $AB + CD = BC + AD$.

$11 + 7 = 9 + AD$, so $AD = 9$ cm.

Perimeter $= 11 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 36$ cm (also $= 2(AB + CD) = 2 \times 18$).

questions.solution_md: Opposite sides of a circumscribed quadrilateral have equal sums, so the perimeter is twice either sum.

questions.stem_md: Prove that the line drawn perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through the centre of the circle.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the tangent at $P$ be $l$, and let $PX \perp l$ at $P$. Suppose $PX$ does not pass through the centre $O$.

By the tangent–radius theorem, $OP \perp l$ as well. Then $OP$ and $PX$ are two **different** lines through $P$, both perpendicular to $l$. This is impossible: through a point of a line there is only one perpendicular to it.

So $PX$ coincides with $PO$, i.e. it passes through the centre.

questions.solution_md: Proof by contradiction using the uniqueness of the perpendicular at a point.

marking_scheme.step: Uniqueness of the perpendicular gives the conclusion

questions.stem_md: A circle is inscribed in an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC = 13$ cm and $BC = 10$ cm. It touches $BC$ at $D$ and $AB$ at $F$. Find $BD$ and $AF$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the tangent lengths from $A$, $B$, $C$ be $x$, $y$, $z$: $x + y = 13$, $y + z = 10$, $z + x = 13$. Adding: $x + y + z = 18$.

So $BD = y = 18 - 13 = 5$ cm and $AF = x = 18 - 10 = 8$ cm. ($D$ is the midpoint of $BC$, as expected by symmetry.)

questions.solution_md: Each tangent length is the semi-perimeter minus the opposite side.

questions.stem_md: $PQ$ is the tangent at $P$ to a circle with centre $O$ and radius $6$ cm, and $Q$ is a point on it with $\angle POQ = 60^\circ$. Find $OQ$ and $PQ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\angle OPQ = 90^\circ$ (tangent $\perp$ radius).

$\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{OP}{OQ}$, so $OQ = \dfrac{6}{1/2} = 12$ cm.

$\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{PQ}{OP}$, so $PQ = 6\sqrt3 \approx 10.39$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: Right angle at P; OQ = 12 cm

questions.stem_md: Ravi is told that the tangent $PA$ is drawn from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, $OA = 6$ cm and $OP = 10$ cm. He writes: "$PA = \sqrt{OA^2 + OP^2} = \sqrt{136}$ cm." Find his mistake and the correct length.

answer.model_answer_md:
In $\triangle OAP$ the right angle is at $A$ (tangent $\perp$ radius), so the **hypotenuse is $OP$**, not $PA$. Ravi treated $PA$ as the hypotenuse.

Correctly, $PA = \sqrt{OP^2 - OA^2} = \sqrt{100 - 36} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The side opposite the right angle (at the point of contact) is the hypotenuse.

questions.stem_md: A circle is inscribed in $\triangle ABC$ with $BC = 8$ cm, $CA = 10$ cm and $AB = 12$ cm. Find the lengths of the tangents drawn from $A$, $B$ and $C$ to the circle.
Two circles have the same centre $O$. A chord $AB$ of the larger circle touches the smaller circle at $M$. Prove that $AM = MB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$OM$ is a radius of the smaller circle and $AB$ touches it at $M$, so $OM \perp AB$.

In right triangles $OMA$ and $OMB$: $OA = OB$ (radii of the larger circle) and $OM$ is common. By RHS, $\triangle OMA \cong \triangle OMB$, so $AM = MB$.

questions.solution_md: Radius ⟂ tangent, then RHS congruence (equivalently: the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord).

questions.stem_md: From a point $P$, $25$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $15$ cm, tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn. Find the length of the chord $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$PA = \sqrt{25^2 - 15^2} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ cm.

By symmetry ($\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$), $AB \perp OP$; let them meet at $M$, so $AB = 2AM$.

Area of right $\triangle OAP$ in two ways: $\dfrac12 \times OA \times PA = \dfrac12 \times OP \times AM$, so $AM = \dfrac{15 \times 20}{25} = 12$ cm.

Hence $AB = 24$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Alternatively $OM = \dfrac{OA^2}{OP} = \dfrac{225}{25} = 9$ cm and $AM = \sqrt{225 - 81} = 12$ cm.

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. Show that $OP$ bisects $\angle APB$, and that $\angle AOP = 90^\circ - \dfrac12\angle APB$. Hence find $\angle AOB$ when $\angle APB = 48^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
In $\triangle OAP$ and $\triangle OBP$: $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$, $OA = OB$, $OP$ common. By RHS they are congruent, so $\angle APO = \angle BPO = \dfrac12\angle APB$: $OP$ bisects $\angle APB$.

In $\triangle OAP$: $\angle AOP = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - \dfrac12\angle APB = 90^\circ - \dfrac12\angle APB$.

With $\angle APB = 48^\circ$: $\angle AOP = 90^\circ - 24^\circ = 66^\circ$, and $\angle AOB = 2 \times 66^\circ = 132^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Check: $132^\circ + 48^\circ = 180^\circ$ ✓.

questions.stem_md: A circle with centre $O$ and radius $4$ cm is inscribed in a quadrilateral $ABCD$ in which $\angle A = 90^\circ$. The circle touches $AB$ at $P$ and $AD$ at $S$. Prove that $APOS$ is a square, and find $AP$ and $OA$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\angle OPA = \angle OSA = 90^\circ$ (radius $\perp$ tangent) and $\angle PAS = 90^\circ$, so $\angle POS = 360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ$: all four angles of $APOS$ are right angles.

$OP = OS = 4$ cm (radii) and $AP = AS$ (tangents from $A$), so adjacent sides are equal: with four right angles, $APOS$ is a square.

$AP = OP = 4$ cm, and $OA$ is its diagonal: $OA = \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2} = 4\sqrt2 \approx 5.66$ cm.

questions.solution_md: A rectangle with two adjacent sides equal is a square.

questions.stem_md: A circle is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ right-angled at $B$, with $AB = 8$ cm, $BC = 15$ cm and $AC = 17$ cm. Find the radius of the circle.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the circle (centre $O$, radius $r$) touch $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ at $F$, $D$, $E$. As in a square corner, $BFOD$ has four right angles and $OF = OD = r$, so it is a square and $BF = BD = r$.

Then $AE = AF = 8 - r$ and $CE = CD = 15 - r$. Since $AE + CE = AC$: $(8 - r) + (15 - r) = 17$, so $23 - 2r = 17$ and $r = 3$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Check with area: $\dfrac12 \times 8 \times 15 = 60$ and $r \times$ semi-perimeter $= 3 \times 20 = 60$ ✓.

questions.stem_md: A parallelogram $ABCD$ circumscribes a circle. If $AB = (3x + 1)$ cm and $BC = (5x - 7)$ cm, find $x$ and the perimeter of $ABCD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Since $ABCD$ circumscribes a circle, $AB + CD = BC + DA$. In a parallelogram $CD = AB$ and $DA = BC$, so $2AB = 2BC$, i.e. $AB = BC$ (a rhombus).

$3x + 1 = 5x - 7 \Rightarrow 2x = 8 \Rightarrow x = 4$.

Each side is $3(4) + 1 = 13$ cm, so the perimeter is $4 \times 13 = 52$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Sanjay says: "Any line perpendicular to a radius of a circle is a tangent to the circle." Using a circle of radius $10$ cm and the line perpendicular to a radius $OA$ at its midpoint $M$, show that he is wrong, and state the correct result.

answer.model_answer_md:
$OM = 5$ cm and the line is perpendicular to $OA$ at $M$. Its distance from $O$ is $5$ cm $< 10$ cm, so it cuts the circle. The points where it meets the circle are at distance $\sqrt{10^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt3 \approx 8.66$ cm from $M$ on either side: two points, so the line is a **secant**, not a tangent.

**Correct result:** the line perpendicular to a radius **at its endpoint on the circle** is a tangent (its distance from the centre equals the radius).

questions.solution_md: Step 1: the line is perpendicular to $OA$ at $M$, so its distance from $O$ is $OM = 5$ cm. Step 2: $5$ cm is less than the radius $10$ cm, so the line meets the circle twice and is a secant. Step 3: a line perpendicular to a radius is a tangent only when it passes through the end of the radius on the circle.

questions.stem_md: In the figure, $AB$ is a diameter of a circle with centre $O$, $AC$ is a chord with $\angle BAC = 32^\circ$, and the tangent at $C$ meets $AB$ produced at $D$. Find $\angle BCD$ and $\angle ADC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$OA = OC$, so $\angle OCA = \angle OAC = 32^\circ$. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, so $\angle OCB = 90^\circ - 32^\circ = 58^\circ$.

$\angle OCD = 90^\circ$ (tangent $\perp$ radius), so $\angle BCD = 90^\circ - 58^\circ = 32^\circ$.

In $\triangle ACD$: $\angle ACD = 32^\circ + 90^\circ = 122^\circ$, so $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 32^\circ - 122^\circ = 26^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Check: the exterior angle $\angle COD = 2 \times 32^\circ = 64^\circ$, and in right $\triangle OCD$, $\angle ODC = 90^\circ - 64^\circ = 26^\circ$ ✓.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

(b) A tangent is drawn from a point $Q$ that is $41$ cm from the centre of a circle of radius $9$ cm. Use (a) to find the length of the tangent.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Given:** a circle with centre $O$ and a tangent $XY$ at the point $P$. **To prove:** $OP \perp XY$.

**Proof.** Take any point $Q$ on $XY$ other than $P$, and join $OQ$. $Q$ must lie **outside** the circle: if it lay on or inside the circle, $XY$ would meet the circle at a second point and be a secant, not a tangent. So $OQ$ meets the circle at a point $R$ between $O$ and $Q$, and $OQ = OR + RQ > OR = OP$.

Thus $OP$ is shorter than $OQ$ for every other point $Q$ of $XY$: $OP$ is the shortest distance from $O$ to the line. The shortest segment from a point to a line is the perpendicular, so $OP \perp XY$.

(b) $\angle OPQ = 90^\circ$, so the tangent length is $\sqrt{41^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{1681 - 81} = \sqrt{1600} = 40$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Every other point of the tangent is outside the circle, so the radius to the point of contact is the shortest segment, hence perpendicular.

marking_scheme.step: OQ > OP for every Q ≠ P

questions.stem_md:
(a) Prove that the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

(b) Tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn from $P$ to a circle, with $PA = 10$ cm and $\angle APB = 60^\circ$. Find the length of the chord $AB$ and the perimeter of $\triangle PAB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Given:** a circle with centre $O$; $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from the external point $P$. **To prove:** $PA = PB$. **Construction:** join $OA$, $OB$, $OP$.

**Proof.** $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$ (tangent $\perp$ radius). In right triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$: hypotenuse $OP$ is common and $OA = OB$ (radii). So $\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$ (RHS) and $PA = PB$ (CPCT).

(b) $PA = PB = 10$ cm, so $\angle PAB = \angle PBA = \dfrac{180^\circ - 60^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ$: $\triangle PAB$ is equilateral. Hence $AB = 10$ cm and the perimeter is $30$ cm.

questions.solution_md: RHS congruence of the two right triangles with the common hypotenuse OP.

marking_scheme.step: Right angles at A and B

questions.stem_md:
(a) A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is drawn to circumscribe a circle. Prove that $AB + CD = AD + BC$.

(b) In such a quadrilateral, $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = (x + 4)$ cm, $CD = 9$ cm and $DA = (2x - 1)$ cm. Find $x$, the lengths of $BC$ and $DA$, and the perimeter.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let the circle touch $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ at $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$. Tangents from an external point are equal, so $AP = AS$, $BP = BQ$, $CR = CQ$, $DR = DS$.

Adding: $AP + BP + CR + DR = AS + BQ + CQ + DS$, i.e. $(AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)$, so $AB + CD = AD + BC$.

(b) $6 + 9 = (x + 4) + (2x - 1) \Rightarrow 15 = 3x + 3 \Rightarrow x = 4$.

$BC = 8$ cm, $DA = 7$ cm. Perimeter $= 6 + 8 + 9 + 7 = 30$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Check: $AB + CD = 15 = BC + DA$ ✓.

questions.stem_md:
A circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$ is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ right-angled at $C$, with legs $BC = a$, $CA = b$ and hypotenuse $AB = c$.

(a) Prove that $r = \dfrac{a + b - c}{2}$.

(b) Prove that the area of the triangle equals $r \times s$, where $s$ is half the perimeter.

(c) For $a = 12$ cm, $b = 35$ cm and $c = 37$ cm, find $r$ by both results and check that they agree.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let the circle touch $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$. $\angle ODC = \angle OEC = \angle DCE = 90^\circ$ and $OD = OE = r$, so $ODCE$ is a square and $CD = CE = r$.

Then $BF = BD = a - r$ and $AF = AE = b - r$. Since $AF + FB = c$: $(b - r) + (a - r) = c$, so $r = \dfrac{a + b - c}{2}$.

(b) Join $OA$, $OB$, $OC$. The radii to the points of contact are perpendicular to the sides, so
area $= \dfrac12 ar + \dfrac12 br + \dfrac12 cr = r \times \dfrac{a + b + c}{2} = rs$.

(c) By (a): $r = \dfrac{12 + 35 - 37}{2} = 5$ cm.

By (b): area $= \dfrac12 \times 12 \times 35 = 210$ cm², $s = \dfrac{12 + 35 + 37}{2} = 42$ cm, so $r = \dfrac{210}{42} = 5$ cm ✓.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) uses the square at the right-angle corner and equal tangents; part (b) splits the triangle into three triangles of height r.

marking_scheme.step: Tangent lengths a − r, b − r and r = (a + b − c)/2

questions.stem_md:
$PQ$ is a chord of length $16$ cm of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $10$ cm. The tangents at $P$ and $Q$ meet at $T$.

(a) Prove that $OT$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$.

(b) Find the distance of the chord from the centre.

(c) Find $OT$ and $TP$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $TP = TQ$ (tangents from $T$) and $OP = OQ$ (radii). So both $T$ and $O$ are equidistant from $P$ and $Q$, and the line $OT$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$. Let it meet $PQ$ at $M$: $PM = MQ = 8$ cm and $OM \perp PQ$.

(b) $OM = \sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm.

(c) In $\triangle OMP$ and $\triangle OPT$: $\angle OMP = \angle OPT = 90^\circ$ and $\angle O$ is common, so they are similar (AA). Hence $\dfrac{OT}{OP} = \dfrac{OP}{OM}$, giving $OT = \dfrac{100}{6} = \dfrac{50}{3} \approx 16.67$ cm.

$TP = \sqrt{OT^2 - OP^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2500}{9} - 100} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1600}{9}} = \dfrac{40}{3} \approx 13.33$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: O and T equidistant from P and Q: perpendicular bisector

questions.stem_md:
A circle with centre $O$ is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. It touches $BC$ at $D$, $CA$ at $E$ and $AB$ at $F$.

(a) Prove that $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

(b) Prove that $A$, $O$ and $D$ lie on one straight line.

(c) If $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm, find the radius of the circle and the length $AF$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Equal tangents: $AF = AE$, $BF = BD$, $CE = CD$. Since $AB = AC$, $AB - AF = AC - AE$, i.e. $BF = CE$. Hence $BD = CD$: $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

(b) $OD \perp BC$ (radius $\perp$ tangent). In isosceles $\triangle ABC$, the line from $A$ to the midpoint $D$ of $BC$ is also perpendicular to $BC$. Through $D$ there is only one perpendicular to $BC$, so $DO$ and $DA$ are the same line: $A$, $O$, $D$ are collinear.

(c) $BD = 6$ cm, so the altitude $AD = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8$ cm and the area is $\dfrac12 \times 12 \times 8 = 48$ cm². Semi-perimeter $s = 16$ cm, so $r = \dfrac{48}{16} = 3$ cm.

$AF = s - BC = 16 - 12 = 4$ cm. (Check: $AO = 8 - 3 = 5$ and $AF = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4$ ✓.)

questions.solution_md: The incircle touches the base of an isosceles triangle at its midpoint, on the axis of symmetry.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Both OD and AD perpendicular to BC at D

options.text_md: the ropes are tied to the same bucket

all radii of a circle are equal
the peg is on the perpendicular bisector of the well

children.solution_md: PA and PB are tangents from the same external point P, so they are equal. (Equal radii are used inside the proof, but they are not the reason by themselves.)

children.stem_md: Find the length of each rope, PA, in metres.

answer.model_answer_md: $OP$ splits $OAPB$ into two congruent right triangles, each of area $\dfrac12 \times 3.3 \times 5.6 = 9.24$ m². Area $= 2 \times 9.24 = 18.48$ m².

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Show that $OP$ bisects the angle between the two ropes, and that $\angle AOB + \angle APB = 180^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
In right triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$: $OA = OB$ (radii), $OP$ is common, so they are congruent (RHS) and $\angle APO = \angle BPO$: $OP$ bisects $\angle APB$.

In quadrilateral $OAPB$, $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$, so $\angle AOB + \angle APB = 360^\circ - 180^\circ = 180^\circ$.
